After you pay the annual Medicare Part B deductible—estimated around three hundred dollars in twenty twenty-seven—Plan G covers one hundred percent of Medicare-approved Part A and Part B cost sharing, including Part B excess charges. While you still need a separate Part D drug plan, Plan G gives you maximum predictability with zero routine doctor copays.

Scene 4: Plan N & The $60–$100/Mo Savings Rule
1:48 – 2:38
HeyGen Spoken Script: Next is Plan N, which offers strong coverage at a lower monthly premium in exchange for three specific trade-offs. Just like Plan G, you pay the annual Part B deductible first, plus up to twenty dollars for certain office visits and up to fifty dollars for an emergency room visit that does not admit you to the hospital. Plan N also does not cover Part B excess charges, though fewer than two percent of Medicare doctors charge them. As a rule of thumb, Plan N makes the most sense when it saves you at least sixty to one hundred dollars a month over Plan G.

HeyGen Spoken Script: Now let us look at High Deductible Plan G, which carries a three-thousand-fifty-dollar annual deductible in twenty twenty-seven. Remember, Medicare still pays its normal eighty percent share first, and your twenty percent cost sharing counts toward that three-thousand-fifty-dollar ceiling, after which the plan pays one hundred percent. Because monthly premiums are dramatically lower—often seventy-five dollars a month versus two hundred dollars for standard Plan G—you can save fifteen hundred dollars a year in premiums. Even better, if you are on a Medicare Advantage plan paying three-hundred-dollar outpatient copays toward a seven-thousand-dollar out-of-pocket limit, High Deductible Plan G can often lower your total annual cost while giving you nationwide provider freedom.

HeyGen Spoken Script: However, High Deductible Plan G is only a good fit if you have savings set aside and will never hesitate to visit the doctor because of the deductible. That brings us to the biggest myth in Medicare: the belief that because Plan G benefits are standardized by law, you should automatically buy the cheapest policy. While the plan letters are standardized, the insurance companies behind them are not. If a carrier prices artificially low just to grab market share, they often hit policyholders with steep rate increases later—and once you are seventy-two or seventy-eight with health changes, medical underwriting in most states can prevent you from switching carriers.
